content: In specific populations, such as men who have sex with men and sex workers, vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is one of the most common causes of vulvovaginitis, affecting approximately 70–75% of women at least once or multiple times during their lifetime. In about 90% of cases, VVC is caused by the fungus Candida albicans, while non-albicans species account for the remaining 10%. Candidiasis is typically of endogenous origin and is not generally considered a sexually transmitted infection (STI), although transmission of Candida species between sexual partners is possible. Bacterial vaginosis (BV), on the other hand, results from an imbalance in the vaginal microbiome and is the most common cause of vaginal discharge globally. The prevalence of BV varies by region, with estimates ranging from 23% to 29% among women of reproductive age. BV is associated with an increased risk of gynecological and obstetric complications, including preterm delivery, spontaneous abortion, and a heightened risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV and other STIs. Although the exact causative agents of BV remain uncertain, it is often linked to an overgrowth of specific pathogens, such as Gardnerella species. BV has been associated with sexual behaviors, including having new or multiple male sexual partners, female sexual partners, and lack of condom use, suggesting possible sexual transmission, though it is not classified as an STI. Certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV) cause anogenital warts, also known as condylomata acuminata. These are benign growths characterized by exophytic, papular, or flat lesions in the anogenital area. HPV types 6 and 11 are responsible for approximately 90% of anogenital warts. While these lesions are typically not problematic due to their size, they often require repeated treatment due to frequent recurrences, with cosmetic concerns being the primary issue. To reduce the burden of STIs and prevent complications, it is essential to provide high-quality prevention, diagnostic, and treatment services. This requires the development of evidence-based guidelines for treatment and comprehensive case management, including screening, diagnosis, treatment, and care. Accessible and affordable treatment is crucial for managing infections caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and Candida albicans, as well as for addressing BV and anogenital warts. The World Health Organization (WHO) last updated treatment recommendations for these infections in 2003 and again in 2021. However, there is a pressing need to review and update these guidelines based on recent evidence, reflecting advancements in diagnostic and therapeutic technologies and addressing the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance. Among these pathogens, Mycoplasma genitalium is particularly concerning due to its significant antibiotic resistance, especially to macrolides and fluoroquinolones. This resistance increases the risk of persistent infection and transmission and is strongly associated with serious reproductive health issues, such as non-gonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and infertility. BV, T. vaginalis, and C. albicans are significant as they are the most common causes of vaginal discharge. Additionally, anogenital warts are prevalent and caused by specific HPV types, making HPV a common STI. Developing evidence-based treatment recommendations for these infections and their associated conditions is essential. The objectives of these guidelines are to provide evidence-informed guidance on treating infections caused by T. vaginalis, M. genitalium, and C. albicans; to offer guidance on managing BV and anogenital warts caused by HPV; and to support countries in updating their national guidelines to achieve the 2030 targets of the global health sector strategy on STIs. These guidelines are intended for STI prevention and control program managers, frontline health workers, and community health workers involved in managing STIs. They are also relevant for organizations working with key populations disproportionately affected by STIs, such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, transgender individuals, and people living with HIV. The development of these guidelines followed WHO's rigorous procedures, including systematic reviews and the use of the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to assess evidence. Recommendations were formulated by a diverse group of experts, including health professionals, researchers, and representatives of affected populations. The guidelines also highlight the importance of managing conflicts of interest during their development. The recommendations prioritize evidence-based interventions for managing infections caused by T. vaginalis, M. genitalium, and C. albicans, as well as BV and anogenital warts. These recommendations apply to all adults and adolescents, including pregnant and breastfeeding individuals, people living with HIV, and key populations at higher risk of STIs.
